And after these things God will bring everything into judgment, where the pastor of souls is compelled to render accounts for each one; and if he has been negligent in this world, he is damned more severely. Therefore it is safer to flee humbly from the care and rule of souls than to usurp it arrogantly. For if each person in that dreadful judgment can scarcely suffice to render account for his own life, how will he answer for so many thousands committed to him? O how well he lives who lives for himself. It seems good and pleasant among men to live in this world as a bishop, abbot, pastor, or any prelate; but who will be able to consider how terrible the end of a negligent man is? For a most severe judgment will be made against those who rule, and the mighty will suffer mighty torments. He passes well who lives simply, to whom nothing of earthly honor is entrusted. For before God the shepherd, the earthly shepherd will have to be presented to render account. Here already the crisis of final condemnation threatens, where the account of a badly administered stewardship is demanded, and the blood of many sheep is required from the hand of one shepherd. What will the unskilled shepherd then be able to answer to the charges, who was negligent in the care of the sheep? He must necessarily fall silent, because he has nothing to answer.

[c ij] He who has been appointed ruler of souls must teach no less by example than by speech. For only the man who does what he teaches can rebuke avarice and luxury in word. He is a delicate master who disputes about fasting with a full belly. Therefore life must be sought before doctrine, because it teaches more fully by deed than by speech. For the demonstration of example is the most excellent kind of teaching. And Jesus himself first did, and afterward taught. For he teaches with the greatest authority whose speech is confirmed by the witness of his work. The ruler’s speech easily benefits his subjects if it is supported by honorable conduct. But he who teaches well and lives badly destroys himself by the sentence of his own mouth, and does not turn his subjects away from evil instruction.

Consider also how dangerous the care of souls is, especially in these times, when iniquity abounds everywhere and the charity of many has grown cold. For the days are evil, and men are slow toward justice; the whole world lies in wickedness, and faith is rare on the earth. Amid these things the word of God is despised by the people; even among religious persons discipline is neglected; priestly authority is contemned. Lay life, liable to many sins and crimes, neglects the remedies of divine mercy and, intent on deceits and frauds, despises the conduct of priests. And unless the ruler of souls diligently announces to the people committed to him their crimes and the penalties due for sins, he will also be guilty of their blood before God. And after these things God will bring all things into judgment, where he compels pastors of souls to render accounts for each one, and he will condemn more heavily those who were negligent in this world.

Therefore it is safer to flee humbly from the care and rule of souls than to usurp it arrogantly. For if each person in that dreadful judgment will scarcely suffice to render an account of his own life, how will he answer for so many thousands committed to him? O how well he lives who lives for himself. You see that bishops, abbots, pastors, or any prelates hold a good place among men in this age; but it is enough to consider how terrible the end of a negligent man will be. For a most severe judgment will be made upon those who are in charge, and the mighty will mightily suffer torments.

He passes well who lives simply, to whom nothing of earthly honor is committed, to whom no care of souls is entrusted. For pastoral care is never without danger as long as one lives in this world. And in this, too, there is a very great sea of dangers: when the soul has been separated from the body by death, the earthly pastor must be presented before God, the supreme pastor, to render account. A hard point of final damnation threatens, when an account of stewardship badly administered is demanded, and the blood of many sheep is required from the hand of one pastor. What, then, will an unskilled pastor be able to reply to the charges, since he was negligent in the care of the sheep? He must fall silent, because he has no answer.

Be diligent in examining all the mysteries of the Scriptures. And if any uncertainty occurs to you as you read, know that you must refer it to the interpretations of the elders. You have nearby the school of the most ancient city of Trier, in which there is an abundance of learned men, to whom you can have recourse in the ambiguity of questions. Let gold not be dearer to you than knowledge, because the fruit of wisdom is eternal, but the use of riches is brief and momentary. Let there be no one who prevents your saving study: not mother, not brother, not kinsman, not sister. Do the work of an evangelist; learn what you are to teach, lest you exist as both shepherd and idol. You are one man and have no second; for whom, then, would you store up riches? Live temperately. Do not visit weddings and immoderate banquets, because they strip the mind of virtues and leave the purse empty of coins. Buy for yourself, from the alms offered, books of divine Scripture, so that, taught by constant reading of them, you may be able worthily to instruct the people committed to you, and to raise yourself by contemplation to heavenly things. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and it will exalt you before God and men. Do not contend with the pleasures of the flesh; restrain the impulse of anger, and never forget death.

What sort of priest he ought to be in his inner conduct. Chapter seven.

Since indeed it is not enough for a minister of Christ to lead an honorable life before men unless he also strives to appear clean from every crime before God, I exhort you to direct your heart in the fear of the Almighty and never admit any thoughts against God. For a priest of God must be holy in mind and body, and clean in thought. Hence the Lord says: Be holy, since I am holy, the Lord your God, who sanctify you. And Peter, the chief apostle, says: You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. First, let charity hold a place in your heart, for it is the fullness of the law and the consummation of the prophets. For the greatest of all virtues is charity, which consists in love of God and neighbor. God must be loved with the whole heart for his own sake, and the neighbor for God’s sake. No one truly loves God if he hates his neighbor in the faith. For Christ is God and man. Therefore he does not love the whole Christ who hates a human being. God accepts no good work unless the flame of charity has kindled it on the altar of the heart. For charity holds the chief place among the virtues. Humility follows it, which is remembered as the guardian of the virtues. So great is the excellence of this virtue that all glory quickly perishes unless humility preserves it. be strengthened by the foundation of humility. For holy Pope Gregory says: “He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind. For where he is seen to be carrying something, there he is more gravely blinded.” Therefore the greatest ornament of a priest is charity, and the most precious pearl in his garment is humility. You too, brother, express these twin virtues in yourself, and you will be a fruitful preacher in the Church of God. Whatever you say, you will easily persuade your hearers if you have charity and humility in your heart and diligently show them in your work.

Let cursed ambition have no place in your heart; once it has invaded a mind, it so blinds it that it brings on forgetfulness of God and of one’s own salvation. Be a Christian lover of men and an enemy of vices. Keep the commandments of God, and do not neglect ecclesiastical sanctions. Honor all men for God’s sake, and never deem anyone worthy of contempt. What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Flee the flatteries of the rich, and never indulge sinners. Deny yourself to your own desires, so that you may become a disciple of Christ. Chastise your body, according to the Apostle, bringing it into servitude. Spurn delights; love chaste fasting. Be dutiful toward the poor. Feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, free the captive, console the sorrowful, bury the dead.

Do not love the world; do not seek riches; do not run after vanities. For no one serving as God’s soldier entangles himself in secular affairs. Do injury to no one, but learn patiently to bear injury inflicted on you, after the example of your Lord, who, hanging on the cross, prayed for his persecutors, that they might not perish. Have peace with all men; have concord and unanimity only with the devout. Do not be proud and arrogant, not sleepy and lazy, not given to wine and much eating, not a slanderer and one who rashly judges anyone. Guard your actions at every hour, and let the memory of future things always turn in your thought. For Scripture says: “Son, remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Therefore always think that you will die; fear the day of judgment; dread the torments of hell. If you do these things, you will easily overcome all temptations of the flesh.

Spurn the pleasures of the world, so that you may be able to enter rejoicing into the joys of heavenly blessedness. Do not deceive your soul: no one can rejoice here with the world and afterward reign with Christ. For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. Therefore, having spurned present things, let us hasten with every desire toward eternal joys. With all watchfulness guard your heart, because from it life proceeds. If you have been overtaken by some sin, do not delay to seek the remedies of penitence and to cleanse yourself in confession through true contrition. Strive to enter into life by the narrow way, that is, not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, to hate the world, and to live by the spirit. You have been called to serve God as a soldier against the vices of the flesh. Do not rest before victory; do not withdraw from the fight, because no one will be crowned unless he is victorious. In this life there is no certain victory, but continual battle. He who perseveres to the end will be saved. A man will be tested at his end. The life of a good man upon earth is warfare. For you are a soldier of the highest king; it is not permitted you to desert his contest. A good soldier follows his king wherever he goes.

Where, then, is your king? In heaven. Why do you not follow him? What are you doing on earth, if you are a soldier of that heavenly king above? Why, then, do you not follow your own king? For he himself says: “He who ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be.” Let him follow, he says, not with the steps of the feet, but with the steps of the affections. The Apostle also says: “No one serving as God’s soldier entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has pledged himself.” Therefore, just as those who serve an earthly king obey all his commands and are ready and prompt wherever they are sent, offering no excuse on account of wife or children, so the soldier of Christ must obey his commands in all things and make no excuse at all.

You therefore, who await the unfading crown of victory, labor like a good soldier of Jesus Christ. Let no care of earthly anxiety weigh you down; let no enticement of fleshly pleasure touch your mind. Nothing is happier than the soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised; nothing is more laborious, because he daily places his life in danger; nothing is stronger, because he conquers the devil; nothing is weaker, because he overcomes the flesh. Let not household choke you, nor kinship impede you, nor the flesh constrain you. I want you to be without anxiety, so that you may freely think on the things that are God’s. Go naked and unencumbered to heaven, because naked your mother bore you, and naked the earth will receive you.

Love what you do not lose; contemn what you cannot hold; seek that in which you may rejoice happily forever. Live in such a way that you do not fear to die. A good conscience has not deserved death, because through it it knows that it will come to the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland.

You now have, most loving brother, what you asked of me. You have some pattern of good conduct on which you may imprint yourself. You have a rule of holy exhortation to which you can diligently have recourse. I have done what I could, not as much as I wished. For the rest, live according to the Gospel and the constitutions of the holy fathers, in which the whole form of Christian perfection is seen. Farewell, remembering us.

From Spanheim, on the Kalends of April, in the year 1486.

Here ends the little book of Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, On the Life of Priests. that is, not to carry out
